On Sat, Aug 27, 2011 at 9:36 AM, Bertram, Alexander <al...@bedatadriven.com> wrote:
Hi Mehmet,

I'm not sure why your second test doesn't run (do you get a stack trace?) but more generally you have to be careful with the signatures because often the internal primitives don't match what you're used to calling from R because the R base library includes an outer function that does argument processing.

So for example, if you open an R-2.x repl and type 'mean', you'll see that it's actually an R-language closure:

> mean
function (x, ...) 
UseMethod("mean")
<environment: namespace:base>

This closure dispatches based on the class of x, either to mean.default or mean.data.frame, etc.

If you look at mean.default you'll see that the na.rm argument is handled at the R-language level:

> mean.default
function (x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...) 
{
    if (!is.numeric(x) && !is.complex(x) && !is.logical(x)) {
        warning("argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA")
        return(NA_real_)
    }
    if (na.rm) 
        x <- x[!is.na(x)]
    if (!is.numeric(trim) || length(trim) != 1L) 
        stop("'trim' must be numeric of length one")
    n <- length(x)
    if (trim > 0 && n) {
        if (is.complex(x)) 
            stop("trimmed means are not defined for complex data")
        if (any(is.na(x))) 
            return(NA_real_)
        if (trim >= 0.5) 
            return(stats::median(x, na.rm = FALSE))
        lo <- floor(n * trim) + 1
        hi <- n + 1 - lo
        x <- sort.int(x, partial = unique(c(lo, hi)))[lo:hi]
    }
    .Internal(mean(x))
}
<environment: namespace:base>

The closure applies the na.rm and the trim functions and then calls the "internal" function which takes a single argument. 

Renjin reuses whole the R-language base package from R-2.10, so we just have to replace the internal functions that are written in C in the original interpreter.

Another point is that currently you can only use the @NamedFlag annotation in combination with an @ArgumentList annotation (see the implementation of c() or the [ ] operators)

This is because in general, R primitives use only positional argument matching and ignore argument names. (This is why many R primitives are wrapped in closures-- the closures handle arg matching, default values, etc, and then pass the processed args to the primitive:

> grep
function (pattern, x, ignore.case = FALSE, perl = FALSE, value = FALSE, 
    fixed = FALSE, useBytes = FALSE, invert = FALSE) 
{
    if (!is.character(x)) 
        x <- structure(as.character(x), names = names(x))
    .Internal(grep(as.character(pattern), x, ignore.case, value, 
        perl, fixed, useBytes, invert))
}
<environment: namespace:base>

However, in the C implementation, each function handles argument processing independently and so is not always consistent.

the @ArgumentList and @NamedFlag are meant to support the family of primitive functions that use a variable number of arguments and some named flags. 

HTH,

Alex

On Fri, Aug 26, 2011 at 3:11 PM, Bertram, Alexander <al...@bedatadriven.com> wrote:
Hi Mehmet,

Regarding the arguments, I've tried to abstract away the argument checking and conversion away from the actual methods so that implementation is a bit cleaner. There is a class called RuntimeInvoker that does this at runtime using reflection (slow) and a class called WrapperGenerator that actaully generates the code at compile time (faster). The WrapperGenerator is still a work in progress and can't generate wrappers yet for all methods, but you can see the generated sources in core/target/generated-sources/r-wrappers

So to implement sort() for other vector types, you can either create an overload for the numeric vectors, like:

 public static Vector sort(DoubleVector x, boolean decreasing)  {
 }
  
 and renjin will choose this at runtime based on the arguments (vectors are widened implicitly, so the method above would catch IntVector and LogicalVector as well) or you could widen the argument type of the existing method:
   
    public static Vector sort(AtomicVector x, boolean decreasing)  

   and implement the algorithm generically (you may want to add a compareElement function to the AtomicVector interface then)  

   Regarding the raw types, I haven't touched them at all, so yes if you wanted to implement the raw functions you could create a new AtomicVector subclass and a corresponding VectorType. 

  Great that you're digging into the code!  Keep the questions comming!

  Alex

On Fri, Aug 26, 2011 at 11:46 AM, Bertram, Alexander <al...@bedatadriven.com> wrote:
Hi Mehmet,

Great! Yes a small first patch but a very useful first patch! 

I think the question about random numbers is a good one. My own feeling is that an R program that runs "correctly" on R-2.x should also run "correctly" on renjin. So I think as long as most R programs don't make too strong of an assumption about what they're getting from the RNG, an alternate implementation from commons math should be sufficient. But I also haven't looked closely at this issue and there may be some specific types of RNGs that are not implemented by commons math and may need to be ported from the C implementations.

It is also a question of priority... My own perfernce is to have first a broad coverage of R functionality implemented, and then to narrow the focus to specific issues of performance or ultra-correctness. The rationale being that a slow renjin that can run 90% of R programs is more useful than a very fast renjin that can only run 30% of R programs. 

But the ultimate success of this project is highly dependent on having a strong team of active committers so I am very open to your ideas and priorities!

Best,

Alex

    @Test
    public void matrixByRow() {

        assertThat(eval(".Internal(matrix(c(1,2,3,4),2,4,TRUE,NULL))"), equalTo(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4)));

added for matrix primitive's byrow= parameter. It seems it is not implemented, i think for the performance issues. I changed Combine.java as:

file: Combine.java
______________________________
public static SEXP matrix(Vector data, int nrow, int ncol, boolean byRow, Vector dimnames) {
        Vector.Builder result = data.newBuilder(0);
        int i = 0;

        if (!byRow) {
            for (int col = 0; col < ncol; ++col) {
                for (int row = 0; row < nrow; ++row) {
                    int sourceIndex = Indexes.matrixIndexToVectorIndex(row, col, nrow, ncol) % data.length();
                    result.setFrom(i++, data, sourceIndex);
                }
            }
        } else {
            for (int row = 0; row < nrow; ++row) {
                for (int col = 0; col < ncol; ++col) {
                    result.setFrom(row + (col * nrow), data, i % data.length());
                    i++;
                }
            }
        }
        result.setAttribute(Symbol.DIM, new IntVector(nrow, ncol));
        return result.build();
    }


Yes, it is only a start for me. But i believe i can do more.

All the best.

> >> Hi Mehmet,
>
> >> I'm not sure why your second test doesn't run (do you get a stack trace?)
> >> but more generally you have to be careful with the signatures because often
> >> the internal primitives don't match what you're used to calling from R
> >> because the R base library includes an outer function that does argument
> >> processing.
>
> >> So for example, if you open an R-2.x repl and type 'mean', you'll see that
> >> it's actually an R-language closure:
>
> >> > mean
> >> function (x, ...)
> >> UseMethod("mean")
> >> <environment: namespace:base>
>
> >> This closure dispatches based on the class of x, either to mean.default or
> >> mean.data.frame, etc.
>
> >> If you look at mean.default you'll see that the na.rm argument is handled
> >> at the R-language level:
>
> >> > mean.default
> >> function (x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
> >> {
> >>     if (!is.numeric(x) && !is.complex(x) && !is.logical(x)) {
> >>         warning("argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA")
> >>         return(NA_real_)
> >>     }
> >>     if (na.rm)
> >>         x <- x[!is.na(x)]
> >>     if (!is.numeric(trim) || length(trim) != 1L)
> >>         stop("'trim' must be numeric of length one")
> >>     n <- length(x)
> >>     if (trim > 0 && n) {
> >>         if (is.complex(x))
> >>             stop("trimmed means are not defined for complex data")
> >>         if (any(is.na(x)))
> >>             return(NA_real_)
> >>         if (trim >= 0.5)
> >>             return(stats::median(x, na.rm = FALSE))
> >>         lo <- floor(n * trim) + 1
> >>         hi <- n + 1 - lo
> >>         x <- sort.int(x, partial = unique(c(lo, hi)))[lo:hi]
> >>     }
> >>     .Internal(mean(x))
> >> }
> >> <environment: namespace:base>
>
> >> The closure applies the na.rm and the trim functions and then calls the
> >> "internal" function which takes a single argument.
>
> >> Renjin reuses whole the R-language base package from R-2.10, so we just
> >> have to replace the internal functions that are written in C in the original
> >> interpreter.
>
> >> Another point is that currently you can only use the @NamedFlag annotation
> >> in combination with an @ArgumentList annotation (see the implementation of
> >> c() or the [ ] operators)
>
> >> This is because in general, R primitives use only positional argument
> >> matching and ignore argument names. (This is why many R primitives are
> >> wrapped in closures-- the closures handle arg matching, default values, etc,
> >> and then pass the processed args to the primitive:
>
> >> > grep
> >> function (pattern, x, ignore.case = FALSE, perl = FALSE, value = FALSE,
> >>     fixed = FALSE, useBytes = FALSE, invert = FALSE)
> >> {
> >>     if (!is.character(x))
> >>         x <- structure(as.character(x), names = names(x))
> >>     .Internal(grep(as.character(pattern), x, ignore.case, value,
> >>         perl, fixed, useBytes, invert))
> >> }
> >> <environment: namespace:base>
>
> >> However, in the C implementation, each function handles argument
> >> processing independently and so is not always consistent.
>
> >> the @ArgumentList and @NamedFlag are meant to support the family of
> >> primitive functions that use a variable number of arguments and some named
> >> flags.
>
> >> HTH,
>
> >> Alex
